summary:
Health Engine is an experimental health monitoring application designed to support astronauts during space missions. It combines computer vision, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), and health data tracking to help monitor physiological indicators in environments where continuous access to medical infrastructure and communication with Earth may be limited.

The application uses a camera-based approach to estimate heart rate by analyzing subtle color variations in facial skin regions. It also provides a health journal for recording blood pressure, temperature, sleep duration, mood, and symptoms, alongside measurement history combined with visual analytics.

By combining camera-based monitoring (Machine Vision algorithm) with structured health records and an offline-first approach, Health Engine aims to make routine health observations more accessible, organized, and useful for identifying changes in astronaut well-being. The project supports preventive health monitoring and research-oriented data collection rather than medical diagnosis.
details:
The application uses a computer vision pipeline to estimate heart rate through remote photoplethysmography (rPPG).

  1. A camera captures a live video stream of the astronaut's face.
  2. MediaPipe detects facial landmarks and identifies suitable regions, including the forehead and cheeks.
  3. OpenCV extracts color information from these regions across consecutive video frames.
  4. Signal processing algorithms analyze periodic color variations associated with blood volume changes.
  5. The application estimates heart rate and displays the result together with signal quality information.

The health journal complements camera-based measurements by allowing users to record blood pressure, body temperature, sleep duration, mood, and symptoms. Measurement history and graphical representations help users observe changes over time.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Health Engine aims to:

  • Support regular health observations during space missions.
  • Reduce dependence on specialized equipment for experimental heart-rate estimation.
  • Organize physiological measurements and self-reported health information.
  • Provide historical data for identifying potential changes in well-being.
  • Support local data collection when communication with Earth is unavailable.
  • Improve awareness of health-related risks associated with isolation, radiation, microgravity, and altered sleep cycles.

Technologies and Tools

The proposed technical architecture includes:

  • Tauri and Rust: Desktop application environment and system-level functionality.
  • React and TypeScript: User interface development.
  • Python: Computer vision and signal processing.
  • OpenCV: Camera access and video frame processing.
  • MediaPipe: Facial landmark detection and region selection.
  • NumPy and SciPy: Numerical computation and digital signal processing.
  • SQLite: Local database and persistent health records.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Health Engine is the combination of camera-based rPPG estimation, health journaling, visual monitoring, and offline-first data management in a unified desktop environment.

Instead of focusing exclusively on a single measurement, the application aims to connect physiological observations with daily health records and historical trends.

The modular architecture also allows future integration of additional sensors, improved signal processing algorithms, and external data synchronization systems.

Factors Considered

During development, the team considered several constraints:

  • Limited and potentially unstable communication with Earth.
  • Camera quality, lighting conditions, and user movement.
  • Reliability and quality assessment of rPPG signals.
  • Local data persistence and privacy.
  • The need to distinguish experimental measurements from medically validated results.
  • The physiological and psychological challenges of long-duration space missions.

Health Engine is an experimental monitoring and research-support concept. Its camera-based heart-rate estimation is not a certified medical measurement and requires further validation under controlled conditions.
